rules.classification: Spectroscopic classes and alert or messenger labels are different definitions and are not compared; two active classes differ when neither label refines the other (for example 'SN Ia' and 'SN Ia-91T' agree); an earlier value from the same provider is a revision.
rules.host: Two proposed hosts agree when their names match after case and spacing are ignored or one name is among the other's NED cross-identifications; otherwise they are an identity ambiguity. Association probabilities are not computed.
rules.photometry: Only exactly compatible photometry (same epoch, band, system, method, calibration and direct/difference state, two or more providers) is compared. The limiting magnitude or flux that a provider reports alongside a detection is that epoch's detection threshold, not a non-detection, and is not compared with the detection; a detection brighter than another provider's non-detection limit at the same epoch is a status conflict. A group is listed only when it is still inconsistent under these rules; at most 10 groups per event, most significant first.
rules.position: Two positions with no stated uncertainty are inconsistent when they are more than 2 arcsec apart; when one states an error radius, the separation is compared with 3 times that radius.
rules.redshift: Two redshifts with no stated uncertainty are inconsistent when they differ by more than 0.005 (about 1,500 km/s); transient and host redshifts are different definitions and are listed, not compared; host redshifts of differently named hosts are an identity ambiguity.
rules.revision: A retracted row, or a superseded row of the same provider whose value differs beyond the property's rule, is a revision or retraction; a revision within the rule is consistent; the earlier value stays visible.
rules.sigma: Two values that both state an uncertainty are inconsistent when they differ by more than 3 combined standard deviations (uncertainties added in quadrature; a stated position error radius is treated as one standard deviation).

rules.classification: Spectroscopic classes and alert or messenger labels are different definitions and are not compared; two active classes differ when neither label refines the other (for example 'SN Ia' and 'SN Ia-91T' agree); an earlier value from the same provider is a revision.
rules.host: Two proposed hosts agree when their names match after case and spacing are ignored or one name is among the other's NED cross-identifications; otherwise they are an identity ambiguity. Association probabilities are not computed.
rules.photometry: Only exactly compatible photometry (same epoch, band, system, method, calibration and direct/difference state, two or more providers) is compared. The limiting magnitude or flux that a provider reports alongside a detection is that epoch's detection threshold, not a non-detection, and is not compared with the detection; a detection brighter than another provider's non-detection limit at the same epoch is a status conflict. A group is listed only when it is still inconsistent under these rules; at most 10 groups per event, most significant first.
rules.position: Two positions with no stated uncertainty are inconsistent when they are more than 2 arcsec apart; when one states an error radius, the separation is compared with 3 times that radius.
rules.redshift: Two redshifts with no stated uncertainty are inconsistent when they differ by more than 0.005 (about 1,500 km/s); transient and host redshifts are different definitions and are listed, not compared; host redshifts of differently named hosts are an identity ambiguity.
rules.revision: A retracted row, or a superseded row of the same provider whose value differs beyond the property's rule, is a revision or retraction; a revision within the rule is consistent; the earlier value stays visible.
rules.sigma: Two values that both state an uncertainty are inconsistent when they differ by more than 3 combined standard deviations (uncertainties added in quadrature; a stated position error radius is treated as one standard deviation).

evidence_timeline.summary: We discuss constraints that the X-ray emission from supernovae can place on their progenitor stars. Since almost all X-ray supernovae arise from massive stars, we concentrate on implications for massive stars. These stars lose mass throughout their lifetime in the form of stellar winds. X-ray emission can be used to gauge the wind properties, especially the mass-loss rates, via various techniques. The abundance of various elements formed by nucleosynthesis within the stars, and released in the stellar explosion, can be estimated from X-ray spectra. In many cases, a combination of X-ray light curves and spectra can allow us to extricate the structure and morphology of the surrounding medium formed by pre-supernova mass loss into which the SN shock is expanding.
evidence_timeline.title: What the X-ray Emission from Young Supernovae Can Tell Us About Their Progenitors

evidence_timeline.summary: We report near-infrared YJHs-band photometry of the very nearby Type Ia-CSM supernova SN 2026sqf in NGC 3310, obtained with the MDM InfraRed Astronomy InGaAs Experiment (MIRAGE) instrument on the MDM 1.3-m telescope. MIRAGE is a new robotic YJHs InGaAs imager in routine operations since March 2026 (Ibrahim & De 2026). The observations were carried out on UT 2026 September 20 (MJD 61303.52). We measure magnitudes of Y = 12.122 ± 0.002 AB mag, J = 11.448 ± 0.002 Vega mag, and H = 10.898 ± 0.003 Vega mag. We encourage continued multi-wavelength follow-up observations, particularly infrared spectroscopy to characterize the possible circumstellar dust emission. Further MIRAGE monitoring of SN2026sqf is planned.
evidence_timeline.title: Luminous late-time infrared emission in SN2026sqf detected with MDM/MIRAGE

evidence_timeline.summary: We reclassify SN 2026sqf as a Type Ia-CSM SN, affirming the original proposal by Midavaine et al. (AstroNote 2026-230). Our NOT/ALFOSC spectra reveal features characteristic of Type Ia SNe (Fe III & Si II; v ~ 10,000 km/s) superimposed upon a blue continuum with strong, narrow Balmer emission. Given the low inferred rates of Type Ia-CSM SNe, one is expected at the distance of SN 2026sqf (D=17.8 Mpc) well less than once in a century.

publication_revisions.abstract: We discuss constraints that the X-ray emission from supernovae can place on their progenitor stars. Since almost all X-ray supernovae arise from massive stars, we concentrate on implications for massive stars. These stars lose mass throughout their lifetime in the form of stellar winds. X-ray emission can be used to gauge the wind properties, especially the mass-loss rates, via various techniques. The abundance of various elements formed by nucleosynthesis within the stars, and released in the stellar explosion, can be estimated from X-ray spectra. In many cases, a combination of X-ray light curves and spectra can allow us to extricate the structure and morphology of the surrounding medium formed by pre-supernova mass loss into which the SN shock is expanding.

publication_revisions.abstract: We report near-infrared YJHs-band photometry of the very nearby Type Ia-CSM supernova SN 2026sqf in NGC 3310, obtained with the MDM InfraRed Astronomy InGaAs Experiment (MIRAGE) instrument on the MDM 1.3-m telescope. MIRAGE is a new robotic YJHs InGaAs imager in routine operations since March 2026 (Ibrahim & De 2026). The observations were carried out on UT 2026 September 20 (MJD 61303.52). We measure magnitudes of Y = 12.122 ± 0.002 AB mag, J = 11.448 ± 0.002 Vega mag, and H = 10.898 ± 0.003 Vega mag. We encourage continued multi-wavelength follow-up observations, particularly infrared spectroscopy to characterize the possible circumstellar dust emission. Further MIRAGE monitoring of SN2026sqf is planned.

publications.abstract: We discuss constraints that the X-ray emission from supernovae can place on their progenitor stars. Since almost all X-ray supernovae arise from massive stars, we concentrate on implications for massive stars. These stars lose mass throughout their lifetime in the form of stellar winds. X-ray emission can be used to gauge the wind properties, especially the mass-loss rates, via various techniques. The abundance of various elements formed by nucleosynthesis within the stars, and released in the stellar explosion, can be estimated from X-ray spectra. In many cases, a combination of X-ray light curves and spectra can allow us to extricate the structure and morphology of the surrounding medium formed by pre-supernova mass loss into which the SN shock is expanding.
